question:
The predecessor states only that a function f:V_1->V_2 satisfies f(phi_1(g)v)=phi_2(g)f(v) for every g,v, and asks to conclude f=0 or a representation isomorphism by treating its zero fiber and image as invariant VECTOR SUBSPACES. Assess whether that functional equation alone is sufficient. Give a genuine nonlinear counterexample with F=C, nonzero finite-dimensional irreducible unitary representations of a finite group, with f continuous (indeed it may be holomorphic). Do not escape irreducibility by using a reducible action. Identify exactly which subspace and injectivity steps need linearity; distinguish an invariant subset from a vector subspace.

Then prove the corrected CONDITIONAL algebraic statement: F is a common field, phi_i:G->GL_F(V_i) are F-linear group representations whose only G-invariant F-linear subspaces are0 and V_i, and f is explicitly F-LINEAR in addition to the functional equivariance equation. Prove ker(f) and im(f) are F-linear subspaces, prove their G-invariance, and use irreducibility to show f=0 or f is a bijective F-linear intertwiner. Prove its inverse is F-linear and intertwines in the reverse direction. Here representation isomorphism means this algebraic linear isomorphism, not merely a bijective equivariant function or a claimed homeomorphism.

State which restrictions on F, dimension, finiteness of G, unitarity or topology are actually required by this proof; do not import finite dimension, algebraic closure, characteristic restrictions or closed-subspace-only irreducibility without justification. If a definition admits zero carrier spaces, handle them explicitly without calling a nonzero-vector argument on0 or insisting that the zero/isomorphism alternatives be disjoint. Explain how this linear zero-or-isomorphism result is used by the scalar endomorphism statement in plan105 without claiming the two complete questions are identical.
reference_answer:
The literal functional-equation statement is false. Let G={+1,-1} with multiplication, V_1=V_2=C, and phi_i(epsilon)z=epsilon*z. This is a one-dimensional nonzero complex representation and therefore irreducible: the only complex-linear subspaces are0 and C. It is unitary; with the discrete topology G is finite and compact and its action is continuous. The map f(z)=z^3 is an entire, hence continuous, function with f(epsilon*z)=epsilon^3*z^3=epsilon*f(z), so it satisfies exactly the displayed functional equivariance. It is nonzero, but f(1)=f(omega)=1 for omega=(-1+i*sqrt(3))/2!=1 and omega^3=1. Thus it is not injective and cannot be a representation isomorphism. It is also not complex-linear: f(2)=8!=2*f(1). Continuity, holomorphicity, finite dimension and unitary irreducibility do not recover the missing linear-map hypothesis.

Two variants locate the proof failures precisely. In the same sign representation h(z)=z^3-z is equivariant and entire, but its zero fiber is{-1,0,1}; it contains1 while1+1=2 is not in it, since h(2)=6. That G-invariant zero fiber is not a vector subspace, so irreducibility cannot be applied to it. In the cube example the zero fiber happens to be{0} and its image is C, yet f is not injective: the implication ker(f)={0}=>injective uses linearity, namely f(v-w)=f(v)-f(w), and is not a set-theoretic fact.

The image-subspace assertion can also fail under an actual continuous compact-group action. Let G=U(1) act on C by u*z and let q(z)=z/(1+|z|^2). Then q(u*z)=u*q(z), q is continuous and the one-dimensional unitary representation is irreducible. Its image is the closed disk of radius1/2: r/(1+r^2) lies in[0,1/2] because (r-1)^2>=0, with equality at r1, and on r in[0,1] it continuously attains every radius in that interval. This nonzero bounded disk is not a complex vector subspace. The example is not claimed holomorphic; the finite-group polynomial examples already meet the stronger holomorphic requirement. Functional equivariance does preserve the zero fiber and image as SETS under the group action, but it does not supply their vector-space closure.

For the corrected theorem let f be F-linear over the specified common field. Its kernel K contains0; if v,w are in K and a,b in F then f(av+bw)=a f(v)+b f(w)=0, so av+bw lies in K. Its image I contains f(0)=0; if y=f(v),z=f(w), then ay+bz=f(av+bw) is again in I. These are the vector-subspace facts missing above, not consequences of equivariance alone.

Equivariance now gives f(phi_1(g)v)=phi_2(g)f(v)=0 when v is in K, since each representation operator is linear and maps0 to0. Thus K is G-invariant. Likewise phi_2(g)f(v)=f(phi_1(g)v) belongs to I, so I is G-invariant. Stability for all g, including g^(-1), also gives equality of the translated subsets if that version of invariance is used. These facts establish the actual hypotheses of algebraic irreducibility.

If f=0 the first alternative holds. Otherwise some v has f(v)!=0, so K!=V_1 and I!={0}. Irreducibility forces K={0} and I=V_2. For linear f, f(v)=f(w) implies f(v-w)=0 and hence v=w; image V_2 is surjectivity. Thus f is a bijection. If y=f(v),z=f(w), uniqueness of preimages gives f^(-1)(ay+bz)=av+bw=a f^(-1)(y)+b f^(-1)(z), proving inverse linearity. For any y=f(v), f^(-1)(phi_2(g)y)=f^(-1)(f(phi_1(g)v))=phi_1(g)v, proving f^(-1)phi_2(g)=phi_1(g)f^(-1). This is a representation isomorphism in the linear sense.

This conditional proof works over any common field, with no algebraic closure, characteristic, finite-group, finite-dimensional, unitarity, inner-product or continuity requirement. It uses algebraic irreducibility (all invariant linear subspaces), not merely absence of proper CLOSED invariant subspaces in an infinite-dimensional topology. It proves an algebraic inverse, not an extra topological inverse theorem. If either carrier is0, its only linear map to/from the other carrier is zero and the zero alternative applies. If both are0 that map is also an isomorphism, so the alternatives need not be exclusive. If irreducibility is conventionally defined only for nonzero spaces, these degenerate cases are simply outside that convention, not an eigenvector justification.

Plan105 uses this linear zero-or-isomorphism result on f-lambda*I after obtaining an eigenvalue. That is a genuine shared subproof and requires the shift itself to be linear. Classifying all commuting endomorphisms as scalars additionally needs the appropriate eigenvalue hypothesis, supplied there by nonzero finite dimension and algebraic closure. The two full targets are therefore related by a dependency, not proved aliases, and no global deduplication or new graph theorem follows from sharing the counterexample or argument.

rubric.criterion: Refutes functional equivariance alone using an explicit nonlinear continuous/holomorphic map on a genuine finite-group complex irreducible unitary representation; identifies invariant-subset versus linear-subspace closure and the failure of zero-fiber=>injective without linearity.
Under the QUESTION'S explicit common-field F-linearity condition, proves kernel and image vector-subspace closure and their G-invariance using the correct domain/codomain representations.

Applies algebraic irreducibility only after proving subspace hypotheses, and for nonzero f proves injectivity and surjectivity; establishes a linear, reverse-intertwining inverse rather than only a bijective function.

Correctly states the absence of algebraic-closure/characteristic/finite-group/finite-dimensional/topological requirements for this algebraic theorem, handles zero carriers if admitted, and distinguishes the shared104 lemma from105's additional eigenvalue/scalar target without changing any standing convention.

exposition.core_summary: Functional equivariance does not imply linearity, even for entire maps on finite unitary irreps. Once common-field linearity is an explicit conditional premise, invariant kernel/image subspaces yield zero-or-linear-isomorphism; scalar Schur additionally needs an eigenvalue route.

semantic_steps.claim: The literal functional-equation reading is refuted by nonlinear maps on the complex sign irrep; with explicit F-linearity, kernel closure and equivariance give a G-invariant linear subspace.
For nonzero linear f, irreducibility forces ker(f)=0, and linear differences—not the zero fiber alone—give injectivity.
Linearity supplies image-subspace closure and equivariance supplies G-invariance; invariant nonlinear images need not be vector spaces.
Irreducibility forces a nonzero linear image to equal V_2, so the same f is surjective.

The inverse is F-linear and intertwines backwards, giving an algebraic representation isomorphism; zero-space and field/topology boundaries are explicit, and105 uses this as a subproof rather than an alias.

contract_binding.original_question: Let (phi_1, V_1) and (phi_2, V_2) be irreducible representations of a group G and let f: V_1 -> V_2 be G-equivariant, meaning f . phi_1(g) = phi_2(g) . f for all g in G. Prove that either f = 0 or f is an isomorphism (so V_1 ~ V_2). Your proof must show that ker f is a G-invariant subspace of V_1 and that im f is a G-invariant subspace of V_2, and then use irreducibility to force the conclusion.
